name: Greenidge Generation Holdings Inc.

facilities.name: Greenidge Power Plant and Data Center

profile.address: Greenridge Generation LLC Power Plant, Town of Torrey, Yates County, New York, 14441
profile.reading:
The power plant and data center at 590 Plant Road in Dresden, in the Town of Torrey, Yates County, New York, sits on the shore of Seneca Lake and carries one of the longest and most litigated regulatory histories of any facility in this registry. The plant began as a coal-fired generating station that ran for roughly seven decades before shutting down in 2011 amid insufficient regional demand for its power; its owners filed for bankruptcy. In 2014, Atlas Holdings, a Greenwich, Connecticut-based private investment firm, bought the shuttered plant, and with the help of a $2 million New York State grant converted it to burn natural gas, reopening in 2017 as a roughly 107-megawatt gas-fired generator (per its NYS DEC Title V air permit, a generating capacity of approximately 107 MW with a maximum heat input of 1,117 million BTU per hour).

By 2019 the plant had effectively stopped selling power to the grid, and starting in March 2020 its owner, renamed Greenidge Generation, pivoted the site to Bitcoin mining, running its own generators behind the meter to power on-site cryptocurrency-mining computers rather than exporting electricity. Mining capacity grew from just over 14 MW in 2020 toward a stated target of 42.5 MW by mid-2021 and 85 MW by the end of 2022, with the company at one point describing ambitions for 500-plus MW across multiple sites nationally. That growth, and the return of a large fossil generator to near-continuous operation, drew sustained opposition from environmental groups and Finger Lakes-region residents concerned about greenhouse gas emissions, lake-water withdrawal (the plant can pull up to 139 million gallons a day from Seneca Lake through a seven-foot intake pipe and discharge up to 134 million gallons daily into the Keuka Lake Outlet), and thermal impact on the lake.

That opposition fed directly into New York State's permitting record. Greenidge's 2021 Title V air permit renewal application prompted a formal DEC review, public hearings in October 2021, and ultimately a denial on June 30, 2022, on the grounds that continued operation was inconsistent with the greenhouse gas limits in New York's Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act -- a first-of-its-kind rejection nationally tying a specific facility's permit to a state climate law. Greenidge appealed; a state Supreme Court decision in November 2024 overturned the DEC's denial and sent the matter back for further review, and years of adjudicatory hearings, including sessions scheduled into November-December 2025, culminated in a negotiated settlement in which DEC agreed to issue a renewed Title V permit in exchange for Greenidge committing to a 44 percent cut in permitted emissions and a 25 percent cut in actual emissions by 2030 -- again described as a first-of-its-kind term in a New York Title V renewal.

Operationally, the plant has continued running through this dispute, with an interruption after a November 23, 2025 electrical switchgear fire forced an emergency shutdown; no mining hardware was damaged, and the company expected to resume normal operations within a few weeks. Most recently, in 2026, amid weak Bitcoin-mining profitability -- mining costs reportedly exceeding 171 percent of mined Bitcoin's value in the first half of 2026 -- and a $33.1 million loan coming due, the parent company renamed itself Vulcan Infrastructure and Power Inc. in July 2026, relocated its headquarters to Pittsford, New York, and began pursuing a recapitalization while pivoting the Dresden site toward AI and high-performance-computing data center use, describing 64 MW as immediately available for that conversion, an approved 60 MW grid draw, and a pending application for a 200 MW AI data center project at the same location.

reading:
Greenidge Generation Holdings, now renamed Vulcan Infrastructure and Power, is in this registry as an operator whose facility is a power plant first and a computing site second. The site is at Dresden, in the Town of Torrey, Yates County, New York, on the western shore of Seneca Lake. It ran as a coal fired station for roughly seven decades before closing in 2011 and passing through bankruptcy. Atlas Holdings bought the shuttered plant in 2014, converted it to natural gas with the help of a two million dollar New York State grant, and restarted it in 2017. The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation describes it as a primarily natural gas fired generating plant of approximately 107 megawatts with maximum heat input limited to 1,117 million BTUs per hour. The company then directed part of that output to bitcoin mining hardware on the property and took the business public on Nasdaq.

The regulatory file is the substance of this entry. The plant's Title V air permit took effect on September 7, 2016. Greenidge applied to renew it in 2021, and on June 30, 2022 the department denied the renewal on the ground that the plant's greenhouse gas emissions were inconsistent with the statewide limits of the Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act. Greenidge requested a hearing on July 28, 2022, an administrative law judge granted party status to four environmental organizations on September 13, 2023, a state court decision in November 2024 overturned the denial, and an evidentiary hearing had been scheduled to run from November 18 to December 10, 2025. The matter was then settled. The department agreed to issue a five year Title V permit requiring a 44 percent reduction in permitted emissions by 2030 and a 25 percent reduction in actual emissions over the same period, with Greenidge dropping its appeal. The company described the actual emissions condition as the first of its kind in a New York Title V renewal. Nothing in the settlement requires mining to stop.

In 2026 the company rebranded as Vulcan Infrastructure and Power and its Nasdaq ticker changed from GREE to VIP on July 24, 2026, with a stated pivot toward artificial intelligence and high performance computing hosting. Its own figures for Dresden are about 106 megawatts of generation, 60 megawatts of approved non curtailable grid power, and up to 60 megawatts previously allocated to mining equipment, with a further 200 megawatts under study and not approved. Those are generation and grid interconnection numbers, not a critical IT capacity, and no IT load is published. The company reported 104 megawatts energized across its sites, a 654 megawatt development pipeline, a near term target of more than 100 megawatts commercialized for AI and HPC, and a 39.4 million dollar investment led by Machine Investment Group and Atlas Holdings. Governor Hochul's July 2026 executive order pausing discretionary state permits for data centers at or above 50 megawatts may delay the Dresden conversion, and data center concerns have appeared on the Yates County legislature's agenda.
